title: Let finite time change one ordinary priority

sections.title: Understand the distinction
sections.body: Awareness of finitude can clarify a modest present choice without creating a countdown or urgency to control others. A priority changes through performed conduct, not through the intensity of its intention.

sections.title: Complete fictional practice material
sections.body: Jo owns a worn favorite book and has 30 discretionary minutes tonight. Reading and writing a private memory note need 20; optional browsing could use all 30. The book can be handled ordinarily and needs no repair in this case. A friend has not agreed to a call, and no urgent reconciliation is required.

sections.title: Work through the supplied case
sections.body: Choose an available action and its opportunity cost, then identify what a later record would need to show. Keep another person’s availability separate.

sections.title: Try a different case before checking
sections.body: A person promises to reconnect someday after thinking about mortality, but takes no step. May the review describe a repaired relationship?

checks.title: Compare reasoning and review the supplied result
checks.body: Reading and a private note can fit 20 minutes with 10 spare, displacing browsing. Later fiction: Jo writes the note but does not read; only the note occurred. Partial: record the full intended 20 as done. Incorrect: demand an immediate friend call because time is finite. A smaller fulfilled choice may matter without proving transformed priorities.
criteria: Finitude informs a feasible present choice
Intention and changed conduct are distinguished

checks.title: Check the changed case
checks.body: No. It records reflection and an intention only. A welcome bounded invitation might be a later action, with response and repair still separate.
